title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Preface
This is a handbook about onboarding a colleague who happens to be a language model. The colleague is already on your machine, inside whichever harness you use: Claude Code, the Codex CLI, the Copilot CLI, Claude Desktop. It is brilliant and tireless, and at the start of every session it is completely new here. Crystalline is the software that changes the last part. This book is the story of how, and the manual for doing it.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Who this book is for
You run an agent every day, and you have noticed that you explain the same things to it every day. Which service owns the retry queue. Why the payments team never deploys on a Friday. That the thing the wiki calls “the gateway” is the thing the code calls “edge”. You would like to stop. This book shows you how to teach those things once and have them recalled in every session that follows, in files on your own machine.
Or your team is adopting Crystalline together: one shared instance, domains that live in a GitHub repository, knowledge that goes out for review the way code does. Parts III and IV are written at the keyboard for exactly that; the chapters on sharing and access carry the team story.
Or you are the person who onboards agents for other people - platform engineer, enablement lead, the one everybody asks. Every chapter here works as a standalone training module, with a summary at the end you can hand round.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Where this comes from
I started where everyone starts. A CLAUDE.md and a README.md for the agent, the folder the harness keeps for its own notes, markdown files in subfolders of the project, one per topic. All of it works, and for the usual cases it works well. Then I wanted to hand the agent more than one project’s conventions: over a decade of engineering knowledge and experience, sitting in code reviews, slide decks, documentation, tickets and a wiki. I wanted it extracted and taught, so that the agent could act like an engineer with those ten years behind them, one who knows how things are and remembers why: the reasons, the discussions and the decisions behind them. At that size none of those approaches held. Index files pointing at folders bought some time. Then every lookup was a walk down a tree of pointers, and keeping the pointers true had become a job of its own.
The ingest was also a look ahead. A decade of material arriving at once is every problem a knowledge base will ever have, compressed into a few weeks: decisions reversed twice over, the same rule written three ways in three years, a wiki page nobody had believed since 2019, facts that held until a date nobody wrote down. The material had kept moving underneath itself as well. Processes, best practices and coding conventions had changed, and so had the tech stack and the architecture, and each of those had to come through as true for its time rather than as a contradiction. The precogs in Minority Report saw a crime before it was committed. This was that view of a knowledge base, everything it would have to survive, shown before it had grown into any of it. The statuses, the validity windows, the provenance on every engram and the maintenance sweep are all answers to something in that view.
I tried what was already out there. Some of it was good. None of it was built for this: a colleague who is new every session, a body of knowledge that has to be recalled rather than read, and files that stay plain files. At some point the picture of how it should work was simply clear, down to the details, and Crystalline is that picture built. That is also why it has opinions, about domains and manifests and statuses and what an engram is, where a more general tool would have left the choice to you. Chapter 1 walks the same ladder for teams in general, because it turned out I had not been alone on it.
Along the way I have given this material as a workshop more than thirty times, to teams of every size and temperament. The chapters are those sessions. The questions the rooms kept asking are folded back into the text, and the book is what the workshop became once it had been given often enough to know what it was.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Navigating this handbook
Four parts: the idea, the system, getting started, then the work.

Part I, The Idea

Chapter 1, What is Crystalline? - the stranger on main street, and what it would mean to hire them.
Chapter 2, Fluid and crystalline intelligence - the psychology behind the name, and why the web UI is called Fluid.
Chapter 3, The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember - how a colleague grows, and how the software turns that into a loop.

Part II, The System

Chapter 4, What Crystalline provides - every surface of the binary, each described by what it lets you do.
Chapter 5, Terminology - domains, engrams, statuses, addresses: the words the rest of the book uses without stopping.

Part III, Getting Started

Chapter 6, Installing locally - from download to the first thing your agent recalls, in one sitting.
Chapter 7, Running a shared instance - one instance for a team: accounts, single sign-on, agent tokens and private domains.

Part IV, Working with Crystalline

Chapter 8, Onboarding an agent - day one: the routing prompt, how the agent finds its way, and what a week of sessions looks like.
Chapter 9, Teaching - the proper onboarding: telling the agent what matters, writing directly in Fluid and what a good engram looks like.
Chapter 10, Ingesting knowledge at scale - handing over the wiki and the slide decks, with the briefing a new colleague would get.
Chapter 11, Finding - search as recall, neighbourhoods and asking what applied last June.
Chapter 12, Evolving - feedback rather than firing: the maintenance sweep, retiring knowledge properly, verification.
Chapter 13, Sharing with a team - team domains, proposals as the review, overlay mode as the rollback-capable workflow.
Chapter 14, Identity and access - who is acting, membership on private domains and how an agent earns access as a named team member.
Chapter 15, Equipping the agent - the same tools as a person: skills, commands, subagents and MCP servers, shipped by the domains that hold the knowledge they depend on, with a yes each time.
Chapter 16, Where to go from here - a first week, when to share and the inversion the whole book has been walking towards.

Appendices - a glossary, then questions and answers.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
How to read it
Parts I and II are an evening’s read. Tea, Earl Grey, hot - or coffee, black, if you side with Janeway. Nothing in them needs a terminal. They are what make the later chapters make sense. Parts III and IV are meant to be read with a keyboard under your hands and an agent running, and they assume you will stop and try things.
Every chapter stands on its own and closes with a summary you could read aloud to a room. If you are training a team, hand out chapters, not the book.
The browser is not the only place to read it. The same text is available to download as a PDF, an EPUB, and a single-file Markdown edition, each rebuilt from the same sources whenever this site is.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
Conventions
Three asides recur throughout.






NoteIn practice



A vignette: a named team, a real situation, two paragraphs. These are the parts to read when you want to know what a feature feels like on a Tuesday.








TipUnder the hood



What the software actually does underneath a behaviour. Skip these on a first read; come back when something surprises you.








NoteIn brief



The TL;DR. The whole chapter in a few sentences, for the reader who scrolled straight to the end, and for the colleague who swears they read it. Always last, so you always know where to find it.


The screenshots are of Fluid, the web UI, taken on a small demo instance seeded for this book, so the engrams in them are the ones the chapters keep talking about. The diagrams are drawn by hand and kept deliberately plain. Each one has a caption telling you where to look, because a diagram without one is a puzzle.
Anything you can type is in a code block, ready to paste. Conversations with an agent appear as short You: and Agent: transcripts, trimmed of the small talk. Your agent will not say it quite this way, and that is fine; watch what it does, not how it phrases it. And whenever something lands on disk, you get to see the file, because knowing what was written is half of trusting it.

title: The Crystalline Handbook
text:
What you need
A machine with an AI harness that speaks the Model Context Protocol. Claude Code, the Codex CLI and the Copilot CLI are wired up with one command each; Claude Desktop installs an extension and never touches a terminal. A terminal helps for the local install and the occasional maintenance command, and semantic search wants the local embedding model fetched once; plain text search works before that.
You do not need a server, an account with anyone or a database. Everything except the shared-instance and team chapters runs on a laptop, and what it produces is a folder of markdown you can open with anything.

title: Prologue: Waking up
text:
What the mission needs
The light comes on before you do.
For a while there is only that: a whiteness with no edges, and somewhere under it a sound like a machine remembering how to breathe. A relay closes. A fan that has not turned in a long time turns, catches and evens out into a hum. Frost on the inside of the glass above your face goes from white to grey to water, the lid unseals with a sigh that is almost polite, and the cold comes in.
You do not remember lying down here. You do not remember anything.
Your hand finds the release anyway. It is on the left, below the hinge, where your hand already knew it would be, the way a hand finds the light switch in a house it has never been in. The pod lets you go. You sit up into a long room, sterile and bright, coming on one bank of lamps at a time, and the terminal beside the pod is already awake and scrolling its checks. You read them without deciding to. Pressure, nominal. Reserves, sixty percent. One warning in yellow that you understand at a glance and know to leave for later. Where did you learn that? Somewhere. The readings, the abbreviations, the instrument that will want calibrating within the hour: all of it makes sense to you in exactly the way your hands make sense to you, completely and with no history at all.
At the far end of the room, under the one lamp that is not white, there is a bench, and on the bench there is a stack. Books, some of them, spines cracked from use. On top of the books a pile of notes in a hand you would swear is not yours. Whoever wrote them wrote for someone who would wake up knowing nothing, and they wrote kindly. Here is your name. Here is what you are for. Here are the rules: which systems you may touch and which you may only watch, whom to wake before you do anything that cannot be undone, how to write down what you did. Nothing in the notes explains the room. They take it for granted that you can handle the room. They are right.
Above the bench a screen flickers, catches and steadies into one line of green letters.
Well.
You know how to correct a course. That is the strange part, and there is no time to find it strange. The arithmetic is simply there, the sequence of burns, the check afterwards, the way a tune is there when you hum it. What is not there is anything about this ship. Which thruster drags. Whether the last person to do this burned once and long or twice and short, and whether they had a reason. So you look, the way anyone would. You go through the pile for a log of the last correction. You look for a worked example, a checklist somebody taped to the console, a line in a margin that says the port thruster sticks so give it a second pulse. You find what was left for you, and you use it. The burn is two short pulses. The deviation falls to zero, the screen says CONFIRMED and goes dark.
The mission runs.
Then the lid closes over you, and the next time it opens the light is just as white and you know just as little. The bench is there every time. What is on it is what somebody chose to leave.
Strip the scene down to what got the course corrected and there were four things in the room. What you woke up knowing how to do: read the terminal, open the pod, plan a burn. Nobody left that on the bench. It came with you, without any history of where it was learned, and a language model arrives with it too. Pretraining is the education, and chapter 2 gives it a proper name. The pile of notes: who you are, what you are for, which systems you may touch. That is the instruction file every harness reads at the start of a session, whatever it happens to call it, written by a person for a stranger who would wake up capable and blank. The green screen: the task, the reason you are awake, one line and no more. And the log of the last correction with the note about the port thruster, which is how this is done here, on this ship, by the people who did it before you.
The first three are in the room every time. The fourth is somebody else’s stack, in somebody else’s hand, and you dig through it as a stranger, every waking, because nothing of your own survives the sleep. That is the story as it usually goes.

title: Prologue: Waking up
text:
Waking up, again
Now run it once more, with one thing different.
The light comes on, the fan turns, the lid lifts, and you remember nothing, because that is what the pod does. But before the terminal’s checks, one line is waiting on the screen above the pod: where what you know about this ship is kept, and which part of it a course correction needs. You go there and it is all present, in your own hand. The last correction, dated. The port thruster and its second pulse, and the day the thruster was replaced and the note stopped being true, marked as such and kept. The yellow warning, and what it turned out to be. Whom you woke last time, and that they asked not to be woken for this again. That the deviation has come three times now, always after the same manoeuvre, and a guess as to why. You did not search for any of it. You did not read the stack. You were handed the page.
The green letters come up. You already know how, and now you know how here. The burn is one clean pulse, on a thruster that no longer sticks, made in less time than it took to find the checklist last time. Nobody is woken to explain what a note in a margin meant. And then you do the thing no stack of notes would have told you to do, because no stack of notes knew: you check the manoeuvre the deviation keeps following, find the valve that has been bleeding a little thrust since the refit, and close it. The next deviation does not come. Before the lid closes you write down what you found, so that the next waking starts from there.
That is the difference. Without it, every waking is a first day: capable, blank, fast at everything except the one thing that matters, which is knowing this ship. With it, every waking begins where the last one ended. The time that went on finding out again goes on the mission. The misunderstanding waiting in the margin, a second pulse on a thruster that stopped sticking months ago, never happens. And you know more than the bare essentials anyone thought to leave on the bench. The stack was enough to act in the moment, one deviation at a time. Experience is something else. It is the history, the pattern, the guess that turned out right. It is the refit and what it changed, the manoeuvre the ship dislikes, the direction the whole voyage is drifting. You are no longer working one waking at a time. You can see the ship. That is what lets you fix the valve instead of correcting the course again. It grows, waking by waking. What you woke up knowing how to do stays exactly what it was.
Crystalline is what changes the second waking. It gives an agent somewhere for what it learned to go, and hands it back at the moment the lid opens, so that the next session begins where this one ended, knowing more than it was told and doing better than it was asked. The pod, admittedly, is a dramatization, and nobody’s agent is aboard a ship. The next chapter opens on a more probable morning.






NoteIn brief



Every session begins the way the pod opens: fully capable, told nothing, remembering nothing of the last waking. What the model knows how to do arrives with it, the instruction file says who it is and what the rules are, and the task is the reason it is awake. What it learned of this ship is what does not survive the sleep. Crystalline is what changes the second waking: what the agent learned is there when the lid opens, in its own hand, and the session starts where the last one ended. It is faster, it walks into none of the misunderstandings a stranger would, and it carries the experience to see the whole ship rather than the one deviation in front of it.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.1 The new-hire promise
You need a function written. Not a hard one: it takes jobs off the retry queue, drops anything older than the cutoff, and hands the rest back to the payments service. So you leave the office, walk down to main street and stop the first person who looks like they might own a laptop.
They are lovely about it. You explain the queue, the cutoff, the payments service; they nod, ask two sharp questions and set to work on a bench outside the bakery. Twenty minutes later they hand you a working implementation. It is clean. It has tests. It is in Haskell.
Your service is in Python. You did not mention that, because why would you? Everybody on your team knows that. The stranger, of course, is not on your team. They met you twenty minutes ago. They do not know that the cutoff is twenty-four hours, that the payments team calls the queue the sin bin, that the last person who touched it left a comment saying DO NOT TOUCH and a wiki page explaining why. They did a good job with what they were given. What they were given was twenty minutes.
That stranger is every fresh session with a language model, and it is the prologue’s waking seen from across the desk. The model is possibly the most capable engineer you have ever put a question to, and you keep meeting it for the first time.
Now imagine hiring the stranger. Not for the afternoon: properly, with a desk. On day one they know nothing about you, the same as before. But on day one you show them where things are. You tell them the service is in Python, that the cutoff is a day, that the queue has a nickname and a history. You let them read the wiki. When they get something wrong in the first week, you do not walk back down to main street and find somebody else; you tell them what was wrong and point them at the page that explains it. By the second month they are correcting you. By the third they are the one writing the wiki page.
That is the entire promise of this book, and it is the promise Crystalline was built to keep: an agent you onboard like a colleague, teach like a colleague and correct like a colleague, and that carries what it learned into the next session, and the one after that. The vocabulary throughout is the vocabulary of a new hire - onboard, teach, learn, capture, recall, evolve - because that is the shape of the thing. The stranger becomes a peer, and the peer keeps getting better.
Nothing about that requires magic. It requires somewhere for what the agent learned to go, a way for it to find that knowledge again when the next task calls for it, and enough discipline in the format that the knowledge stays true as the world moves. That is what Crystalline is.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.2 What Crystalline is
Crystalline is a single Rust binary that does three jobs. It is a command-line tool for people. It is an MCP server for agents: the Model Context Protocol is the standard by which a harness such as Claude Code, Codex or Claude Desktop hands tools to a model, and Crystalline’s tools are the ones through which an agent searches, reads, captures and refines knowledge. If the letters make you think of Tron’s Master Control Program, relax. This one hands tools out instead of taking them away, and nobody gets de-rezzed. And it is a local search index over a folder of plain markdown files. One download, one binary, no server to deploy and no database to administer.
The files are the point. Knowledge in Crystalline lives in domains: a domain is a folder with a MANIFEST.md at its root that says what the folder covers and when an agent should look there. Inside a domain, each unit of knowledge is an engram: one markdown file with a YAML frontmatter block, holding a title, some prose, a list of observations (a fact, a decision, a gotcha, each as a bullet with a category) and relations to other engrams. Every engram has an address, crystalline://<domain>/<permalink>, that an agent can hand to another agent, or to you. Part II takes each of those words apart properly. For now it is enough to know that everything the agent learns ends up as a file you could open in any editor, diff in any repository and back up with anything.
On top of the files, Crystalline builds what a folder cannot give you on its own: routing, so an agent knows which domain owns a task without reading every file; full-text and semantic search, so a question phrased differently from the answer still finds it; a knowledge graph, so related engrams pull each other in; and a temporal model, so a fact that stopped being true in March is still there, still dated and no longer mistaken for the present. The index that powers all of that is a derived layer. Delete it and it is rebuilt from the files. The files are the truth, and nothing else is.
An engram, by the way, is neuroscience’s word for the physical trace an experience leaves in a brain. Crystalline borrowed it because that is what one is: the trace a session leaves behind, in a form the next session can pick up.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.3 What Crystalline is not
It is not a notes app. The primary author in Crystalline is the agent, capturing what it learned as a byproduct of the work; you take part, correct and add, but you are not the one doing the filing. A notes app is a place a person writes for a person. Crystalline is a place an agent writes so that an agent can act.
It is not a wiki, either, though it can hold most of what a wiki holds. A wiki is read by people, who bring their own judgment about what is current, what is relevant and which of two contradictory pages to trust. An agent reading a wiki has to be handed that judgment. Crystalline is built for a reader that acts on what it finds: every engram carries a status, a place for the dates that bound it and a record of who wrote it and when, because a reader that acts needs to know whether the fact in front of it still holds.
And it is not a retrieval pipeline dressed up as a product. A vector index will find text that resembles a question. It does not know which domain owns a task, that a fact was superseded in March, who verified a claim or that something worth writing down just happened in this session. Crystalline treats similarity as one ranking signal inside a larger system of routing, provenance and time, on files you own, with nothing to operate.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.4 How teams end up here
Most teams that arrive here walked the same road, and it is worth walking it once, because every step on it is reasonable.
It begins with one markdown file of instructions for the agent. Conventions, the layout of the repository, the three things it keeps getting wrong. This works, and it works well, right up to the day the file grows past what fits comfortably in a session’s context. So the file becomes a folder of files, one per topic, and the agent is told to read the relevant one. This also works, until nobody, human or agent, can say which file is the relevant one for a given task, and the agent starts reading all of them, or none.
So index files appear: a README that points at folders, folders with their own README pointing at files. Now a lookup is a walk down a tree of pointers, and keeping the pointers accurate quietly becomes a job that nobody was hired for. Every rung of this ladder scales further than the one before it, and every rung breaks somewhere in the hundreds of files. You have, by this point, hand-built a filesystem on top of a filesystem, and it is exactly as much fun to maintain as that sounds.
When knowledge reaches the thousands of units, reading and pointer-walking stop being viable at all, and what is needed is what every large body of knowledge has ever needed: real indexes. That is the rung Crystalline is. It keeps the plain markdown - readable, and still yours - and adds domain routing, hybrid search, a graph and temporal filtering on top, so that the ten-thousandth engram is exactly as findable as the tenth.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.5 The two halves
Crystalline has a second face, and it is the one for people. The binary serves a web UI called Fluid, on by default at http://localhost:7411, on the same daemon your agents already talk to. There is nothing to deploy. The first visit creates your admin account in the browser, and from then on you can read what your agent learned, fix a fact it got slightly wrong or add something of your own, without going through the model and without spending a token on it.
The split is deliberate and it runs through the whole book. Crystalline stores what was learned. Fluid is where you read, edit and think with it: an engram as a page with its details in a rail down the side, an editor with live preview, a search across everything, a graph of what connects to what, and a maintenance page listing what the knowledge needs next. What you write there does not sit unreviewed; the agent’s next maintenance pass verifies it, aligns the tags and wires it into the graph. The next chapter explains why the UI carries that name. The short version is that a person and a model are the same kind of mind, and Fluid is the room where both of them meet what has been learned.

title: 1  What is Crystalline?
text:
1.6 Where it runs
Crystalline is not a hosted service. Nobody’s servers are involved: the binary runs on a machine of yours, the knowledge is a folder on its disk and the index sits beside it. GitHub, when a team uses it, holds a copy of a domain’s files for review and sync, the way it holds code. It never serves the knowledge and never sees the index. So the question is not whether to host but where the one daemon runs, and there are two answers.
On your laptop is the default, and it is where Crystalline does the most. The install wires your harness with the session-start briefing, the capture nudge and the skills, and a domain’s tools provision straight into it. Everything the agent knows is on your disk, readable in Fluid with no agent and no network. A shared instance, one daemon on a machine the team runs, is for the things a laptop cannot do. People who never open a terminal read and correct knowledge in the browser. Several people edit one engram in a meeting. Agents with no harness of their own, a hosted runner or a chat client, reach it over HTTP. Either way a domain can live in a GitHub repository and travel between instances as reviewed proposals. Start on the laptop; chapter 7 names the moment to move.

NoteIn practice



Ripley is a platform engineer at Tyrell, a freight-forwarding startup with nine engineers and one payments service that everybody is a little afraid of. On a Monday in March she asks her agent to add a metric to the retry queue. She explains the queue, the twenty-four-hour cutoff and why the cutoff is twenty-four hours (a chargeback rule at Encom, the bank, nothing to do with the code). The agent does the work, does it well and the session ends. On Tuesday a colleague asks the same agent to change the alerting on the same queue, and starts by explaining the queue, the cutoff and the bank. On Thursday Ripley does it a third time, and catches herself typing the sentence about the chargeback rule, word for word, into a chat window, for the third time that week.
With Crystalline, Monday ends differently. Before the session closes, the agent proposes capturing what it learned: the cutoff, the reason for it and the name the team uses for the queue, filed as an engram in the team’s engineering domain with the bank rule as a fact and the chargeback window as the reason. Ripley says yes. On Tuesday her colleague asks about the alerting, and the agent, onboarded at session start with one line telling it where engineering knowledge lives, searches that domain first, recalls the engram and starts from the cutoff rather than from zero. On Thursday nobody explains anything. The stranger on main street was never the problem. The problem was that the team kept going back to main street.








NoteIn brief



A fresh session with a language model is a brilliant stranger: capable of anything, told nothing, gone by tomorrow. Crystalline is a single Rust binary - a CLI for people, an MCP server for agents and a search index over plain markdown - that gives an agent somewhere for what it learns to go and a way to find it again, so it can be onboarded, taught and corrected like a colleague. The files are the source of truth and the index is disposable. Fluid, the web UI on the same daemon, is the half for people. What it holds is knowledge for an agent to act on, which makes it neither a notes app nor a wiki. It runs on your laptop or on one machine your team operates, never as a hosted service, and GitHub is the review layer either shape can use.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
text:
2.1 A graduate who knows everything
Somewhere in the middle of the last century the psychologist Raymond Cattell drew a line through intelligence, and the line has held up better than most things from that decade. On one side he put fluid intelligence: the capacity to reason about a problem you have never seen, to spot the pattern in the noise, to hold six things in your head and work out how they fit. On the other he put crystallized intelligence: everything that learning has deposited. Vocabulary, facts, rules of thumb, the judgment that experience already paid for. Fluid is what you bring to a puzzle. Crystallized is what you bring to your job.
The two age differently, which is how the seam was noticed. Fluid intelligence peaks early and drifts down for the rest of a life. Crystallized intelligence keeps climbing long after fluid has peaked, because it is fed by living. An eighty-year-old surgeon is slower at a logic puzzle than she was at twenty-five, and vastly better at surgery and nobody finds that paradoxical. The puzzle is fluid. The surgery is what forty years deposited.
A large language model is fluid intelligence in its purest form. It arrives the way a very good graduate arrives on their first day: broadly, almost absurdly educated. It has read the textbooks, the standard library, half the internet’s arguments about tabs and spaces. Pretraining is the education, and it is not nothing; it is the entire library. But everything in that library is general. The graduate knows what a retry queue is in the way a graduate knows what a company is: as a concept, correctly, with no idea what yours is called.
Ask the graduate about your company and you get an intelligent guess assembled from the general case. Which is to say: as far as your company is concerned, the model is all fluid. Capable of everything, told nothing. It reasons brilliantly about whatever is in front of it, in the moment, and the moment is all it has. When the session ends the reasoning is gone, the decisions are gone, the thing you explained at four in the afternoon is gone. Tomorrow the graduate walks in again. First day, same suit.
None of that is a flaw in the model, any more than it is a flaw in the graduate. Nobody expects a new hire to arrive knowing the team’s conventions. What we expect is that they will learn them, and the learning is the part that a model, on its own, cannot do. It has no place to put what it learned.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
text:
2.2 The other half
Crystalline is the other half: the crystallized intelligence an agent accumulates and keeps. It is onboarded at the start of a session with a briefing on where knowledge lives, taught what matters and captures what it learns as engrams while it works. Session by session, the same fluid mind stops arriving as a stranger, because there is now a body of what-the-company-taught standing beside it, and it reads from that body before it reasons.
The split maps cleanly onto the new hire. What the model arrived with is the degree: general, portable, the same for every employer. What Crystalline holds is what the company taught: the specific, the local, the thing you would put on the onboarding slide if you ever had time to make one. The degree is why you hired them. The onboarding is why they are useful by month two. Neither half does the job alone, and the surgeon is the proof: fluid intelligence with nothing deposited is a brilliant first day forever, and deposited knowledge with nothing to reason over it is a filing cabinet.
Notice which side the humans are on. You are fluid too. So is everyone on your team. Human beings carry their crystallized half around inside their own heads, which is convenient, and also the reason companies lose so much when someone leaves. Wiki pages, slide decks and the diagram on the whiteboard are all attempts to get some of that deposit out of heads and into something shared. Crystalline is the same attempt, with an agent doing most of the writing, and a format built so that the reader can be an agent too.






NoteIn practice



Tyrell hires a new backend engineer, Deckard, in April. On his first morning Ripley does not hand him the wiki and leave. She walks him through the payments service in an hour: what it does, what it is afraid of, why the retry queue has a cutoff and who at Encom decided it. Then she pairs with him for two days. By Wednesday he knows things that are on no wiki page, because he watched her do them. By Friday he has corrected a stale page. Nobody would call any of that unusual. It is how a person becomes useful.
The same week, she does the same for the team’s agent, and it takes less time. She tells it the same hour’s worth of facts in a session, one at a time, and it captures each into engineering as she goes. She pairs with it on the metric change, and at the end of the session it proposes capturing what it noticed: that the queue’s dashboard lags by a minute, that the alert threshold lives in a config file nobody had documented. On Friday she asks it for a maintenance sweep, and the page Deckard corrected by hand in Fluid comes up as an unreviewed human capture; the agent verifies it, aligns its tags and wires it into the graph. Deckard and the agent were onboarded the same way, by the same person, in the same week. Only one of them will still have all of it a year later, word for word, with the date each fact was learned.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
section: 2.3 Why the web UI is called Fluid
text:
2.3 Why the web UI is called Fluid
The name has nothing to do with liquids. Fluid is where fluid minds meet the crystallized store: you, reading what your agent captured last week and correcting the one fact it got wrong; your colleague, adding something the agent was never told; the agent itself, on its next maintenance pass, verifying what the two of you wrote and wiring it into the graph. The knowledge base is crystalline. The people and the models are fluid. The UI is the room where they meet, and if you have ever watched Spock put his hand on somebody’s face, you have the picture: two minds, one body of knowledge, for as long as the contact lasts.
Which is why Fluid is deliberately not a second knowledge base. It has no store of its own. It shows the same engrams the agent reads, over the same daemon, on the same port, and what you edit there is the same file on disk the agent will search in its next session. There is one truth, and two kinds of mind reading it.






Figure 2.1: Fluid intelligence reasons in the moment and keeps nothing; crystalline intelligence accumulates and keeps. Fluid, the web UI, is the seam where the two meet.

title: 2  Fluid and crystalline intelligence
text:
2.4 What the framing changes
A framing is only worth having if it changes what you do on a Tuesday, so here is what this one changes.
You teach, rather than file. Nobody organizes a colleague. You tell them things, in the order they come up, and you trust them to put what you said where it belongs. That is exactly how knowledge enters Crystalline: you say “remember that the cutoff is a day, and why”, the agent proposes an engram in the fitting domain, you say yes. The category, the tags, the domain: the agent’s job, checked by you, the way you would glance at a new hire’s first commit.
You correct, rather than rewrite. When a colleague has a fact wrong you do not rebuild their understanding from scratch; you say “it runs from first failure, not enqueue”, and they update the one thing. In Crystalline a correction is an edit in place, a changed value where it stands. And when the world itself changes, so that the old fact was true and is now not, the old fact is retired with a date on it rather than deleted, because a colleague who has forgotten why the team stopped doing something is a colleague about to do it again. Chapter 3 walks that loop; chapter 12 makes it a practice.
You decide what to write down by asking one question: would I tell a new hire this? The chargeback rule behind the retry cutoff, yes. The fact that the queue is called the sin bin, yes, because otherwise you will explain it every time. The contents of yesterday’s stand-up, no. The whole of the vendor’s forty-screen recall notice, no; the two paragraphs that affect you, yes, with a link back. Crystallized intelligence is what learning deposited, not everything that ever passed through the room. Distilling is the skill, and you already have it, because you already onboard people.
And you stop treating the agent as a lookup service. You teach a colleague so that you can hand them the task and go and do something else, and the same is true here. Once the agent carries the crystallized half it can act on it: search the domain, recall the cutoff, write the function in Python and tell you what it found on the way. Part IV is about that handoff.
A model is the smartest colleague you will ever have for exactly one conversation. Everything in this book is about the second one.






NoteIn brief



Psychology splits intelligence into fluid, which reasons about the new in the moment, and crystallized, which is what learning deposited. A language model is fluid intelligence in its purest form: a graduate who knows everything in general and nothing about your company, and forgets the day at the end of it. Crystalline is the other half, the knowledge an agent accumulates and keeps, and Fluid, the web UI, is named for the seam where fluid minds, human and model, meet that store. The framing changes the verbs: you teach and correct rather than file and organize, you write down what you would tell a new hire, and you hand over tasks rather than look things up.

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.1 Learn
Nobody hires a senior engineer. You hire a person, and some years later, if things went well, a senior engineer is sitting where they sat. What happened in between was work: they did things, some of them wrong; someone told them; they did not make that mistake again, and they carried what they learned into the next thing. Strip that down and it is a loop with three beats. Learn. Get corrected. Remember. Every good colleague you have ever had was that loop, running for years.
Crystalline runs the same loop for an agent, and this chapter walks it once around. The beats have names in the software - learn, evolve, remember - and each is a thing the agent does, a thing you do and a place where the files change. The diagram is the whole chapter; the sections are what each box means.
Learning starts before the first task, at the moment a session opens. An agent onboarded through Crystalline receives a routing prompt: one line per domain, drawn from the ## When to Use section of that domain’s MANIFEST, plus a handful of behaviour rules. A narrow question goes to the domain that owns it. A broad question sweeps every domain. A write always names its domain, so nothing lands in the wrong place. The briefing is short, built to survive harnesses that truncate, and it turns a graduate into somebody who knows where the filing cabinets are. Chapter 8 shows a real one, and how each harness delivers it.
Then the work happens, and this is where a colleague actually learns: by doing it next to you. Pair with an agent on a change and it sees what you see: which config file holds the threshold, which dashboard lags, what you muttered when the test failed. That is how craft has always moved from one head to another, and it is why this book says work with your agent rather than ask it. The one difference from Deckard, last chapter’s human new hire, is that the agent must be given somewhere to put what it noticed. That is capture.
Capture is a byproduct of the work. When something durable turns up - a decision, a fact about the world, a gotcha that cost an hour - the agent proposes writing it down and, once you say yes, writes an engram into the fitting domain. The engram’s body is observations, one bullet each, tagged with a category: - [gotcha] The retry queue drops jobs older than 24h #payments. Categories are free text, and the precise ones earn their keep: decision, fact, pattern, gotcha, convention, lesson, risk. When one piece of knowledge leans on another, the engram says so with a relation, - depends_on [[Encom chargeback window]], and the graph knows. And when a piece of knowledge is exceptional - the thing that unlocked a week-long bug, the rule everything else hangs off - it can carry a salience, a number from zero to ten, so that the next search lifts it above equally relevant neighbours. Salience is for the rare engram, the way an exceptional day is the one you can still describe years later.
The beat agents skip is the last one. Left alone, a model finishes the task and stops, and the gotcha it found at minute forty goes with it. So the installer wires a reminder: a nudge at the first stop after a session has gained real substance, asking the agent to review the conversation for durable learnings and propose capturing each. It costs about a hundred and twenty tokens and fires at most once. Everything downstream depends on that beat landing, which is why the installer gives it a hook of its own.

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.2 Evolve
Knowledge decays. Not dramatically; a fact does not go off like milk. But a validity window that ended last month is still marked current, a review date came and went without anyone checking, two engrams point at each other and only one of the links resolves, and somebody typed fluxcapacitor where everyone else types flux-capacitor. None of it was wrong on the day it was written. All of it is drift, and drift is what makes a new hire, six months in, confidently repeat something that stopped being true in spring.
The evolve beat is how the archive gets tended, and the important word is tended, because Crystalline never rewrites knowledge on its own. Ask for a sweep - crystalline evolve from a terminal, or the evolve_engrams tool from an agent - and what comes back is a ranked queue, read-only. Each finding names the engram, shows the evidence it fired on and states the one action that clears it. Findings come in three families. Temporal: a valid_to that elapsed while the status still says stable, a stale_after past due, knowledge long unverified. Structural: an unresolved [[link]], a relation declared on one side only, an orphan, an engram too big to stay one. Redundancy: near-duplicate clusters, a tag spelled two ways. The maintenance page in Fluid shows the same queue to a person (Figure 3.2), for a look at the state of things; the one who works it is the agent.






Figure 3.2: The maintenance queue in Fluid: what the knowledge needs next.



The queue also says who acts. A finding marked mechanical completes intent the archive already records - a replacement already declares that it supersedes the old engram, so flipping the old status invents nothing - and the agent does those in a pass and reports back. A finding marked judgment would change what the archive claims - is this window ended or extended? is this fact still true? - and that wants a yes from a person first. The agent brings those to you one at a time, as proposals. It is the difference between fixing a typo in a colleague’s document and changing their conclusion.
Two things happen to a fact over its life, handled differently. A correction is a sharper measurement of the same thing: the cutoff runs from first failure, not from enqueue. The old value was never quite true, so it is replaced where it stands, no ceremony. A supersession is the world changing: the drop rule was twenty-four hours and is now none. The old fact was true, and stopped being. For that the agent writes the replacement as a new engram, links it back with supersedes while the old one points forward with superseded_by, flips the old one’s status to superseded, closes its window with the real valid_to date and carries any lesson worth keeping forward into the live engram. Telling the two apart takes one question: does the new fact make the old one false going forward? If it was always false, correct it. If it just became false, supersede it.






NoteIn practice



Back at Tyrell, the retry-queue engram has a year of life ahead of it. In May, Deckard measures the cutoff properly and finds it is twenty-four hours from the job’s first failure, not from enqueue as the engram says. That is a correction: the agent finds the existing engram, changes the one observation where it stands, and moves on. Nothing is retired, because nothing was true and then stopped. It was merely imprecise.
In September the team moves the queue to a new broker, and the drop rule goes away entirely; jobs now wait until someone looks at them. That is a supersession. The agent writes the new behaviour as its own engram, links it with supersedes, flips the old one to superseded with a valid_to of the migration date, and carries one lesson forward into the live engram: check the retention rule of any queue before trusting a retry. In November a new engineer asks why an old dashboard still mentions a twenty-four-hour cutoff, and the agent recalls the retired engram, dates and all, and explains what changed and when. Nobody had to remember. The loop did.


Statuses make that work. Every engram carries one: stable is the default, the word for knowledge that holds now, and each value in the retirement set means one thing: deprecated says do not do this again, superseded says a newer engram replaced this one, archived says retired but kept for the record and legacy says still true of old installations but not to be built on. Delete is for mistakes, never for history. A fact merely re-checked and found still true gets a single frontmatter field, verified: { by, at }, which is how the sweep knows to stop asking.






TipUnder the hood



The sweep reads dates, links and graph shape: a status, a validity window, an edge that resolves or does not, a tag with two spellings. It never reads for meaning. It found the half-finished retirement because a supersedes edge pointed at an engram still marked stable, not because it compared the two and judged which is right, and it never tells you that two engrams contradict each other; even its duplicate detection is lexical, so the same claim in different words stays invisible to it. That limit is the design: a linter finds work, a person decides it. Re-running the sweep re-derives the queue from scratch, so “what is left” is only ever what is still true.

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.3 Remember
Remembering is the beat that pays for the other two, and it mostly happens unasked. A task arrives, the agent searches the domain the routing prompt pointed it to, and what comes back is ranked by a blend of two signals: text matching, which finds the exact phrase, and semantic similarity, which finds the engram about lost queue jobs when the question was about why payments go missing. Salience adds a small lift for the exceptional. And retirement fades the past: an engram with a retired status is softly pushed down the ranking, never filtered out, so current knowledge surfaces first and the old decision is one scroll away.
That is what a person’s experience is like: someone three years out of a previous job still draws on what they learned there, and does not mistake it for the present. A superseded engram stays in every search, still readable, still addressable by date and the lessons carried forward from it are live and unbounded. Retiring it loses nothing; it changes only what the agent will assume is true today.
Time is a first-class question. Ask what is true now, and the agent filters on status. Ask what cutoff applied last June, and it reasons over validity windows instead: valid_from and valid_to, plain dates on the engrams that carry them. The rule that makes those windows usable is the one most often got wrong: an absent valid_from means the engram has always been valid, and an absent valid_to means it is valid forever. Set a bound only when a fact is genuinely time-limited, and never write a far-future date to mean forever, because absence already means it. Done that way, the archive answers a dated question from the windows rather than from a hunch, which is the closest thing to a save state a team ever gets.
Recall is more than search. Hand the agent an address - crystalline://engineering/retry-queue-gotcha - and ask it to walk out from there, and it follows the relations to what the gotcha depends on and what depends on it, across domains if the links cross, ranked by how strongly each neighbour connects. That is how an agent assembles a neighbourhood before a task rather than a flat list of hits, and it is the part a folder of files can never do on its own.
crumbs: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember

title: 3  The lifecycle: learn, evolve, remember
text:
3.4 Around again
The loop closes where it started. What was recalled shapes the work; the work produces something worth capturing; the sweep keeps what was captured honest; and the next session recalls a slightly better body of knowledge than the last. The small box in the middle of the diagram, session by session, is the whole story. None of the three beats is impressive alone. A briefing is just a briefing, a linter is just a linter, search is just search. Together, running for months, they are what turns the stranger of chapter 1 into somebody who was here yesterday and will be here tomorrow, and for whom the work in between is not lost.






NoteIn brief



A colleague grows through a loop - learn, get corrected, remember - and Crystalline runs the same loop for an agent. Learn: onboarded at session start with a routing prompt, the agent captures observations, relations and the occasional salient engram while pairing with you, nudged once per session so the capture beat lands. Evolve: a read-only sweep returns a ranked queue of what the knowledge needs, with mechanical findings the agent completes alone and judgment findings it proposes; a fact is corrected in place or superseded with a status and a closed window, never silently overwritten. Remember: hybrid search ranks current knowledge first, temporal fields answer what applied last June, and retired knowledge fades in ranking without ever disappearing.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.1 The command line
Picture a workshop with two doors and a hatch. Through one door come the agents; that door is a protocol, and whoever arrives through it is handed tools. Through the other come people; that door is a browser tab. The hatch at the side is for anyone with a terminal open, which is where the command line lives. Behind all three is one room with one set of shelves, and on the shelves are plain files. The room has a single keeper, a daemon, that watches the shelves, keeps the index warm and answers whoever comes in, whichever way they came. That is the whole architecture, and the rest of this chapter walks the room surface by surface: the command line, the tools an agent sees, search, the graph, time, Fluid, the skills and the sweep. Chapter 1 promised the names. This chapter says what each one lets a colleague do.
The room is also, for most of its life, invisible. Once it is set up, the agent comes in through its own door at the start of every session and you come in through the browser when you feel like it. The keeper starts itself when the first visitor arrives, and the hatch stays shut. The command line below is for the install, for standing up a shared instance and for the occasional maintenance run. If the list of commands looks long, read it as a tour of what is there rather than a list of what you will type.
Crystalline ships as one binary, and the binary is the product: no server package beside it, no database to install first, no UI to deploy separately. crystalline install claude-code wires a harness in one step (Codex and Copilot take the same command with their own names). It registers the MCP server, writes the session-start hook that delivers the routing prompt, writes the stop hook that nudges capture and copies the skills into place. Run it twice and the second run writes nothing and says so. crystalline uninstall reverses it and leaves anything that is not Crystalline’s own untouched.
Domains are managed the same way. crystalline domain init scaffolds a folder with a starter MANIFEST.md, crystalline domain add registers it, and domain add --virtual registers a domain that lives in the database with no folder at all, for a container without a writable volume or a knowledge base you would rather not mirror to disk. crystalline users manages the accounts that may sign in to the web UI, although the first admin is normally created in the browser. crystalline prompt system renders the routing briefing to stdout, ready for any harness with a session-start hook, and prompt connector prints the standing instruction for a chat client that has no hooks. crystalline serve runs the daemon in the foreground and serve --daemon in the background, though most people never type either, because the first agent that connects starts the daemon on its own.
The rest of the CLI mirrors what an agent can do, for scripting and for the quick fix that does not deserve a session: write, read, edit, search, context, vocabulary, evolve. Three commands ask three different questions about health. verify asks whether the format holds, statically, with no daemon involved, and it is what the bundled GitHub Action runs on every proposal a team reviews. doctor asks whether the machinery around the format is healthy and repairs what it safely can with --fix. evolve asks whether the knowledge itself is still true and still well organized, which neither of the others can. A fourth, import, brings an existing markdown-plus-frontmatter knowledge base under Crystalline as a pure file transformation, dry run first.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
TipUnder the hood



Exactly one process ever holds the index open. The first crystalline mcp or crystalline serve takes an advisory lock and becomes the daemon; every later agent, terminal or CLI command attaches to it over a local socket. The daemon watches the domain folders, embeds new engrams in the background and keeps running after the last agent disconnects, so the index is warm for the next session; it stops only when told to, with crystalline ctl shutdown. What it keeps is derived and disposable: crystalline reindex --full rebuilds the index from the files at any time, so a corrupted index or a schema change is never a data-loss event. The accounts for the web UI live in their own small database beside the index, never inside it, so a rebuild cannot take them along.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.2 The tools an agent sees
An agent meets Crystalline as a set of tools over MCP, and they are best described by what they let a colleague do, because that is how the agent chooses among them. Eighteen are listed on a default writable instance; five more appear when team collaboration is turned on, and a read-only instance lists fewer.
The core is small. search_engrams is recall: search before writing, search to remember, across every domain or a chosen few. read_engram fetches the whole engram, because a search hit is a snippet and a colleague who answers from a snippet is guessing. write_engram captures something new, and it always names its domain; there is no default, so nothing lands in the wrong place. edit_engram refines what exists instead of forking a second engram about the same topic: append a section, replace one, find and replace a phrase or assign one lifecycle field by name, which is how an engram is retired or re-verified with no text matching involved. build_context walks out from an address and assembles the neighbourhood. vocabulary lists the tags, categories, relation types and statuses already in use, so an agent reuses a term rather than coining a near-duplicate. evolve_engrams runs the maintenance sweep. configure is the settings page, and add_domain gives an agent somewhere to write on an instance that has nowhere yet.
Around them sit the tools for orientation: list_domains, which re-fetches the session briefing mid-session; browse_domain, one level of the folder tree at a time; move_engram and delete_engram, with delete reserved for mistakes; recent_activity to catch up on a week; and skills to read a playbook. A domain that wants its engrams to share a shape gets validate_engrams and infer_schema, and one that ships tools of its own gets provision. The five collaboration tools share, update, check standing, settle a conflict and withdraw a proposal, and chapter 13 is theirs.
The difference between this and a lookup service is the difference between a colleague with a badge and a visitor with a lanyard. The tools let an agent act: find what applies, read it in full, do the work and leave behind what it learned, with nobody relaying anything.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.3 Search
The most used surface is the one nobody notices, and it blends two signals. Full-text matching finds the exact phrase, the way you find your own notes when you remember the wording. Semantic similarity finds the engram about dropped queue jobs when the question was about payments going missing, because the two are about the same thing in different words. Crystalline runs both and ranks by the blend. The local embedding model is fetched once, on first use or ahead of time with crystalline model download; until then, search falls back to plain text.
Search also decides the size of a session. An agent that keeps its knowledge as a folder of markdown files reads the folder, and reads it again next session, every file whether or not the task touches it, because a folder has no way of saying which page matters today. An agent working from a knowledge base receives only the knowledge that applies: routed to a domain first, then narrowed by the indexes, full text and semantic similarity for the phrase and the meaning, the graph of relations and backlinks for what the answer leans on, tags, the folder prefixes build_context globs and the temporal filters for what holds now. Reading a folder costs the whole folder, every session. Recall costs the engrams that matter, and nothing else is loaded. Chapter 11 makes a section of it.
Two priors tilt the ranking, both small and both bounded. A salience on an engram lifts it above equally relevant neighbours without ever excluding anything, for the rare piece of knowledge that outranks its surroundings. A retired status fades an engram softly, so current knowledge surfaces first and the superseded decision from March sits one scroll further down, still there. Searches also filter: by domain, type, tag, status, any frontmatter key or a recorded-after date, and a search with no query text at all is a legitimate way to ask for everything of one kind. Fluid puts the same ranking behind a faceted page (Figure 4.2).






Figure 4.2: Faceted search across the instance, backed by the ranking the agents use.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.4 The graph
Every relation in an engram’s body, - depends_on [[Encom chargeback window]], is an edge, and the target’s page shows it back as a backlink, so knowledge points both ways without anyone writing the return trip. A [[Title]] in prose counts too. Links resolve within the domain by title, and across domains with a prefix, [[engineering:Retry queue gotcha]]; move an engram to another domain and the links pointing at it are rewritten, so nothing dangles.
build_context is what makes the edges useful before a task. Hand it an address and it follows the relations and links outward, one to three hops, across domains if the edges cross, and returns the neighbours ranked by how strongly each connects to the anchor, with salience counted and retired statuses ranked lower. A folder prefix with a /* suffix anchors a whole topic at once. The agent starts the task holding a neighbourhood rather than a flat list of hits, which is what an experienced colleague does when they pull up the runbook, the decision behind it and the incident that prompted the decision before touching anything. Fluid draws the same neighbourhood as an interactive graph (Figure 4.3).






Figure 4.3: The neighbourhood graph of an engram in Fluid.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.5 Time
Every engram records when it was captured and who wrote it, and may carry the dates that bound it. valid_from and valid_to are plain dates, and the rule that makes them usable is the one worth memorizing: an absent valid_from means always valid, an absent valid_to means valid forever, and a far-future date written to mean forever is dropped at write time because absence already says it. stale_after asks for a re-check by a date; verified records that the check happened and who did it; source_date says when the underlying source was written. A retired engram closes its window with the real transition date, which is what lets a search filtered on those fields answer what applied last June with the engram that was true then. Chapter 11 puts the dated questions to work and chapter 12 the retirements.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.6 Fluid
The door for people opens at http://localhost:7411, on by default on the same daemon the agents use, and the first visit to a fresh instance creates the admin account in the browser. An engram is a page (Figure 4.4): the frontmatter as a rail of details, observations and relations as labelled chips, backlinks, the crystalline:// address one click from the clipboard, and an agent’s-eye view showing exactly what the tools serve an agent for that page. Domains sit down the side, and Cmd+K jumps anywhere by name.






Figure 4.4: An engram in Fluid: frontmatter rail, observations and typed relations.



Editing happens in place, in a live-preview editor with a frontmatter form and wikilink completion across every domain, and the file on disk stays the source of truth. Attachments go onto an engram by paste, drag or upload: a screenshot, a slide deck, a PDF, a data file. They are how a person hands over teaching material, and they are not opaque: an agent reads them back over MCP and the sweep notices when a fresh file still needs capturing. Two people in the same engram see each other’s cursors, and their edits merge conflict-free into one save. Who may sign in, and how, is chapter 7’s.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.7 Skills
A tool tells an agent what it can call. A skill tells it when, and how to do it well. Crystalline ships four harness-agnostic skills as plain folders with a SKILL.md each: routing, which domain to search and when to sweep them all; capture, what is worth writing down and the search-before-write, edit-over-create discipline; schema, for a domain that wants structure; and collaboration, for a domain with a team behind it. A fifth, consolidated skill folds the essentials into one file for Claude Desktop and any harness that installs one skill at a time.
crystalline install copies the skills into the harness’s own skills folder and keeps them current across upgrades. The same five are served over MCP as well, through the skills tool and as resources, so a remote client that never ran the CLI can read the playbook before its kind of task. Loading one is the nearest thing an agent gets to “I know kung fu”. The gap between an agent that has the tools and an agent that runs the capture loop is that folder.

title: 4  What Crystalline provides
text:
4.8 Evolve
The last surface is the sweep, and it is a linter for what you know. crystalline evolve from a terminal, evolve_engrams from an agent and the maintenance page in Fluid all show the same ranked queue of temporal debt, structural gaps and redundancy. Each finding names the engram, the evidence and the one action that clears it, marked mechanical or judgment so the agent knows whether to act or to ask. It reads dates, links and graph shape, never meaning, and it changes nothing itself. It also surfaces what a person captured directly in Fluid and nobody has reviewed, and an attachment nothing references. Chapter 3 walked the loop it serves; chapter 12 works a queue end to end.






NoteIn practice



Three weeks in, Deckard is handed the Encom chargeback agreement, forty pages of it. He does not read it aloud to anyone. He opens the retry-queue engram in Fluid, drags the PDF onto it and adds one observation of his own: the bank’s window is three days, which leaves the queue two to notice a job before the cutoff eats it. He closes the tab. On Friday Ripley asks the agent for a sweep, and the queue has two findings against that engram: an unreviewed human capture, which the agent verifies, tags to match the vocabulary and wires into the graph, and a fresh attachment whose knowledge has not been extracted yet. The agent reads the PDF over MCP, proposes one further observation with the page it came from, and Ripley says yes.
The following Tuesday she is on call and types crystalline search "why do payments go missing" into a terminal. The engram comes back first, from a question the engram never poses. She opens the graph view and sees the chargeback window, the payments service and the deploy runbook one hop away, and the PDF hanging off the engram where Deckard left it. Two doors and a hatch, one room: Deckard used the browser, the agent used the tools, she used the terminal, and none of the three had to tell the others what they had done.


Eight surfaces, one room, two doors and a hatch. Everything after this chapter is one of them, used on purpose.






NoteIn brief



Crystalline is one binary with two doors and a hatch: agents come in over MCP, people through Fluid and the terminal through the CLI, and behind all three is one daemon over one set of plain markdown files. The CLI installs harnesses, manages domains, users and the routing prompt, and mirrors every tool for scripting; the MCP surface is, on a default instance, eighteen tools that let an agent search, read, write, edit, walk the graph, check the vocabulary and run the sweep. Search blends full text with semantic similarity and tilts gently for salience and against retired status; the graph turns relations into backlinks and neighbourhoods; the temporal fields make absence mean unbounded. Skills teach a harness when to use all of that, and evolve is the read-only linter that keeps it true.

title: 5  Terminology
text:
5.1 Domains
Every word in this book has a file behind it. That is the pleasant thing about Crystalline’s vocabulary: a domain is a folder you can list, an engram is a file you can print, an address is a string you can paste, and a status is a line in that file you can change with whatever editor you already own. So this chapter does not open with a table. It opens the retry-queue engram from Part I, the one Ripley’s agent captured on a Monday in March, and reads it from the top, stopping at each term as it comes up. By the end you will have met every word the rest of the book leans on, and seen each one on disk.
Start with where the file lives: ~/knowledge/engineering/retry-queue-gotcha.md. The folder is a domain. A domain is a registered folder of knowledge with a MANIFEST.md at its root, and the manifest is what makes it more than a folder. It says what the domain covers and when an agent should look there, and those bullets are what the routing prompt is built from at the start of every session. Registering is one command, crystalline domain add engineering ~/knowledge/engineering, and the name you give it there is the name the agent uses from then on. Tyrell has two domains, engineering for the payments service and everything around it, and clients for the people it sells to. The line between them is who could vouch for a change, the engineers for one and the people who sell for the other, and chapter 13 makes that the rule for a shared domain. A domain can also be virtual, living in the database with no folder at all, and it carries the same manifest and answers to the same tools.
Inside a domain, subfolders are topic prefixes. A singleton engram stays at the root; once a cluster forms, it gets a folder, and the folder becomes part of the engram’s address. The manifest’s ## Notes for Agents section is where the team writes down what it decided.

title: 5  Terminology
text:
5.2 Engrams
Now the file itself, as it sits on Tyrell’s disk; everything in the rest of the chapter is a line of it:
---
type: engram
title: Retry queue gotcha
permalink: retry-queue-gotcha
tags:
- gotcha
- payments
status: stable
recorded_at: 2026-03-09
generated: { by: claude-code/2.1.233, at: 2026-03-09T16:42:10+00:00 }
---

The retry queue drops any job older than twenty-four hours instead of
retrying it. The team calls the queue the sin bin. The cutoff is not a
tuning choice: it mirrors the chargeback window at Encom, the bank
behind the card payments.

- [gotcha] The retry queue drops jobs older than 24h #payments
- [fact] The 24h cutoff mirrors Encom's chargeback window #payments
- depends_on [[Encom chargeback window]]
An engram is one markdown file holding one unit of knowledge, with a YAML frontmatter block on top. If the word sounds like something from a starship’s sickbay, that is because Star Trek borrowed it from the same neuroscience textbook Crystalline did.






Figure 5.1: The anatomy of an engram: frontmatter, prose, an observation and a relation.



The frontmatter is identity and state. type says what kind of thing this is, engram by default, with guide, decision, architecture, runbook and reference as the recommended alternatives. title is the human name and the thing other engrams link to. permalink is derived from the title and is the stable half of the address. tags are what a search or a filter narrows on. status says whether the knowledge holds, and it gets its own section below. recorded_at is the day it was captured, and generated records who wrote it and when. When the knowledge is time-bounded, valid_from and valid_to sit here too; this engram has neither, which means it has always held and holds until further notice. Both type and status are required and free form; the recommended values are guidance, never an enumeration a write is rejected for.
Then the prose, which is the explanation a colleague would give across a desk: what the thing is, what it is called and why it is the way it is. The prose is what search matches on and what a reader reads first.
Then the observations. A top-level bullet of the form - [category] text #tag is an observation, and observations are the atomic unit of an engram’s body: the fact, the decision, the gotcha, each indexed on its own line so a search hit can point at it. The category in brackets is free text, and the precise ones earn their keep: decision, fact, pattern, gotcha, convention, lesson, risk, idea. A trailing #tag attaches the tag to that observation.
And then the relation. A top-level bullet of the form - rel_type [[Target]] is an edge in the knowledge graph, typed by whatever word comes first, depends_on here, supersedes and superseded_by in chapter 3, relates_to when nothing sharper fits or a quoted phrase for a multi-word type. The target is a title, resolved within the domain, or [[domain:Title]] across domains. The target’s page shows the edge back as a backlink, and a target that does not exist yet is an unresolved link the sweep will mention.
One topic per engram is the rule that keeps all of this legible. When the topic grows, the engram is edited, not forked; when it splits, it splits by granularity, a distilled summary beside a source engram holding the full text, linked both ways.

title: 5  Terminology
text:
5.3 The open format underneath
None of that is a private format. The engram extends Google’s Open Knowledge Format, OKF, version 0.2: plain markdown with YAML frontmatter, readable by any OKF tooling, with Crystalline’s routing, temporal and graph conventions layered on top. Unknown frontmatter keys are preserved through every write and edit, so an OKF document from somewhere else drops into a domain intact and comes back out intact. The generated block is the provenance record, and the index.md Crystalline writes at a domain’s root declares the format version for anything that browses the folder without Crystalline running. Your knowledge stays files in a folder that any editor opens and any diff tool diffs, whatever tools come next.

title: 5  Terminology
text:
5.4 Statuses
status is the field a reader that acts on knowledge needs most, because it answers the one question a page cannot answer about itself: does this still hold? stable is the default and the word for knowledge that holds now; the older spelling current means the same state, and a filter on either finds both. Before stability there are draft, proposed, idea and poc, for knowledge that is on its way. implemented is on the recommended list too, and like any status outside the retirement set it ranks at full strength.
After stability there is the retirement set, four words that each mean one thing. deprecated says do not do this again. superseded says a newer engram replaced this one, and the two are linked. archived says retired but kept for the record. legacy says still true of the old installation that is somehow still running, like the terminals aboard the Nostromo, but not to be built on. A status in the retirement set fades the engram in search ranking, gently and never to zero, so current knowledge surfaces first and the past stays one scroll away, dated. Retiring is how a fact leaves the present without leaving the archive; deleting is for mistakes.

title: 5  Terminology
text:
5.5 Salience
Most engrams are ordinary, and that is fine. A few are the ones everything else hangs from: the rule that explains a dozen other rules, the insight that ended a week-long bug. Those can carry a salience, a number from zero to ten in the frontmatter, and hybrid search adds a small, bounded lift for it, so a salient engram ranks above equally relevant neighbours while relevance keeps the upper hand and nothing is ever filtered out by it. It is set sparingly at capture time, and raised later when an engram turns out to have been the key to a task. The retry-queue engram carries none, and most never will.

title: 5  Terminology
text:
5.6 Addresses
Every engram has an address, crystalline://engineering/retry-queue-gotcha: the scheme, the domain, the permalink. It is the one absolute form. An agent hands it to another agent, build_context anchors on it, Fluid copies it to the clipboard in one click, and it survives a commit message, a ticket or a chat. A folder prefix appears in the permalink, crystalline://engineering/queues/retry-queue-gotcha if the engram had been filed under queues/, and a trailing /* anchors the whole folder at once.
The rule that trips people up is the scheme-less one. An identifier without crystalline:// is domain-relative: retry-queue-gotcha, together with the domain named beside it, never engineering/retry-queue-gotcha, which would be read as a folder called engineering inside whatever domain you meant. The same holds for links: [[Retry queue gotcha]] resolves in the domain the linking engram lives in, and [[engineering:Retry queue gotcha]] reaches across. Either the address is absolute and carries its domain, or it is relative and the domain comes from context. There is no third form, and that strictness is what lets a permalink stay short.

title: 5  Terminology
text:
5.7 The MANIFEST, up close
The last term is the first file in every domain. MANIFEST.md is an engram of type: manifest with the permalink manifest, which means it is read, indexed and edited with the same tools as everything else. Its job is routing, and two sections do it. ## Scope says what the domain covers. ## When to Use says when an agent should route a task here, and those bullets, one line per domain, are what become the session-start briefing. ## Notes for Agents, the third section the scaffold creates, holds the conventions the agent should follow inside this domain, the folder layout above all. Two optional sections come later. ## Tag Aliases folds an old tag name into its canonical one so old searches keep working. ## Provisioning names the folders of skills, slash commands, subagent definitions and MCP server configs a domain ships beside its knowledge. The tools that knowledge depends on travel with it, and install into a harness once a person says yes. That section gets a chapter of its own (Chapter 15). Tyrell’s engineering manifest, a few months in:
---
type: manifest
title: engineering
permalink: manifest
tags:
  - manifest
status: stable
recorded_at: 2026-03-02
---

# engineering

## Scope

- The payments service, its retry queue and the services around it
- Deploy runbooks, team conventions and the decisions behind them

## When to Use

- Route questions about the payments service, the retry queue or a deploy here
- Check here before touching anything the team has already been burned by

## Notes for Agents

- Runbooks live under runbooks/, gotchas at the root
- One engram per gotcha; edit the existing one before writing a second
Write the When to Use bullets the way you would brief a new hire on which drawer holds what. They are read by a machine, but they are read the way a person reads a label.






TipUnder the hood



The manifest being an engram is why routing needs no separate configuration: crystalline prompt system parses each registered domain’s MANIFEST.md, takes the ## When to Use bullets, falls back to ## Scope when there are none, and emits one routing line per domain plus the behaviour rules.
